report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is the best-supported practical answer: CoQ10 has **not been shown reliably to relieve statin-associated muscle discomfort**, so it should not be considered an established treatment.

The strongest negative evidence is a 2020 systematic review/meta-analysis of **seven randomized placebo-controlled trials**. It found no benefit for muscle pain and no improvement in staying on statin therapy. However, the trials were small and clinically heterogeneous, so this is “no convincing evidence of benefit,” rather than proof that nobody can benefit.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021915020301386

Why uncertainty persists: a 2018 meta-analysis reported improvements in pain, weakness, cramps, and tiredness with CoQ10. But differing study selection, small trials, subjective symptom measurement, variable statins/doses and CoQ10 formulations, and likely placebo/nocebo effects make that positive result less definitive.  
https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.118.009835

There is biological plausibility—statins can reduce circulating CoQ10—but lower blood CoQ10 does not establish that supplementation fixes muscle symptoms.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30414615/

**Bottom line:** CoQ10 is generally tolerated, but evidence is conflicting and the better synthesis of placebo-controlled trials does not support routine use for statin muscle discomfort. Muscle symptoms warrant clinician review rather than stopping a beneficial statin on one’s own: assess other causes/interactions and consider a temporary stop/rechallenge, a different statin or dose, or non-statin lipid-lowering treatment when appropriate.
